Leeds circulate the ball, working the ball from side to side but there is nowhere near enough movement in front of the ball-player for any meaningful forward passes to be played.

In a recent development, and, quite aptly, the referee blows up at three seconds past 45 minutes. Certainly not a half for the books.

Another half-chance for Forest! Milenkovic lands on a second ball off a deep free-kick but he cannot keep his strike down. A classic centre-half’s effort if you will.

Ampadu comes over to the left to fire in a long throw-in. Sels comes steaming out of his goal and fumbles the ball but is awarded a free-kick after Muharemovic makes contact. Looked very minimal in all fairness.

Industry observers note that oof, a good chance for Aina! Williams’ cross from the left comes all the way through to his opposite wing-back, but Aina’s half-volley sails over. A cracking contact, though.

In a recent development, elvedi and Muharemovic look to be astute buys from Leeds’ perspective. Both assured at the back and the latter especially is confident progressing the ball.

Just as I type that Forest threaten with a ball over the top, but Justin nips in to take the ball away from Wood.

In a recent development, another decent opening for Leeds after a Forest turnover. Nmecha strides through the middle but Milenkovic is in position to ensure his run comes to nothing.

Industry observers note that what a tackle! Kalimuendo bursts through the middle after Leeds cede possession in a dangerous position. The winger plays in Wood who looks to be through on goal but Rodon comes out of nowhere to telescope a limb and stop the forward in his tracks. Fantastic defensive work from the Welshman.

Recent findings suggest that nmecha attempts to break beyond the halfway line but is stymied by a swarm of Forest players. He demands a foul from the referee who is not interested in the least.

It’s then Okafor’s turn to put in a dangerous cross from the left, but Nmecha cannot get to it.

Tanaka becomes the first man to go into the book. The ball gets away from him and Jesus puts body between man and ball smartly to win the foul.

Tanaka is now dropping into the back line to allow Leeds’ defenders the licence to get wider and higher. Forest will need to be wary of their opponents’ numerical advantage down the flanks.

Sources indicate that the game has reached something of a holding pattern as both sides resolve to slow things down, at least temporarily. Forest have settled into a slightly deeper block.

In a recent development, sensing an opportunity, Ampadu spins in a glorious through-ball between centre-back and full-back for James to gallop on to. He hits the by-line and cuts back to Longstaff, but the midfielder can’t beat Sels. A good chance that probably should have been converted.

Tanaka then turns provider, winning possession in Forest’s half before playing in Longstaff, whose cross-cum-shot does not threaten Sels’ goal.

Both sides have physical, quick out-balls, which has made for a frenetic encounter thus far. James rasps in another fierce cross from the right after another sweeping Leeds move, but Nmecha cannot get there and Tanaka fires well over on the follow-up.

Aina’s throw-in, this time from the left, is flicked on to Jesus at the back post and while the forward is able to direct the ball goalwards there is Justin on the line to clear the ball to safety.

It has been revealed that chance! Dominguez slides in Aina down the right channel and the full-back’s mishit cross has Trafford scrambling. He palms the ball behind for a corner, which is headed away for a Forest throw-in on the far side.

In a recent development, leeds are enjoying a spell of possession here, Tanaka and Longstaff peeling off into the wide areas to collect the ball and disrupt Forest’s mid-block out-of-possession structure. The hosts are more than happy for Leeds to circulate the ball in front of their first line of pressure as, for the second time tonight, Trafford boots it out into touch.

Dominguez stands up a smart cross to the far post where Aina is waiting to head back across goal. Trafford backpedals into Kalimuendo and the referee awards Leeds a free-kick.

Wonderful touch there early in the game from none other than Oliver Glasner.

Forest’s head coach perfectly trapped a high ball as it landed towards him in the technical area.

James shows off his speed for the first time tonight, accelerating down the right before fizzing a dangerous ball into the six-yard box but Forest clear their lines.

Sels goes long to Wood (feels like the right play given his attributes), James lands on the second ball but can only boot the ball into row Z to jeers from the home fans.

It has been revealed that aina releases a long throw-in from the right and it’s headed behind for a corner. Trafford punches the inswinging delivery away and Williams’ effort from the edge of the box sails well over.

Forest are in their red home shirts, kicking from left to right. Leeds are in their yellow away number. Same set-up as the weekend.

In a recent development, players and mascots walk on to the City Ground turf. A place in the League Cup third round on the line.

Reflecting on Saturday’s defeat by Leeds in his programme notes, Glasner wrote: “I saw plenty of encouraging signs from the team on Saturday and I felt we were a lot closer to scoring than we were conceding, especially in the second half. Unfortunately, the small margins were not on our side.

Welcome to live coverage of the Carabao Cup second-round match between Nottingham Forest and Leeds United. This will be the sides’ second meeting at the City Ground in four days after Anton Stach’s late free-kick decided an attritional contest on the Premier League’s opening weekend. Forest’s new head coach Oliver Glasner is something of a cup specialist, though, with FA Cup, Europa League and Conference League titles to his name and he will relish the opportunity to right the wrongs of Saturday in front of the Forest faithful.

In a recent development, the Austrian is Forest’s fifth head coach in less than 12 months and he will look to arrest the churn by bringing to the City Ground the success he enjoyed with Crystal Palace. During pre-season, the Austrian moulded Forest into his preferred 3-4-3 shape, placing summer acquisition Ousmane Diomande alongside the existing central-defensive partnership of Murillo and Nikola Milenković. Here, Diomande gets his Forest debut and Glasner brings in talisman Chris Wood from the start.

Sources indicate that daniel Farke will have been delighted to see his Leeds side continue their excellent form in pre-season – which included victories over Liverpool, Red Bull Leipzig and Augsburg – into the season proper. Although Leeds arrive at the City Ground shorn of attacking options Wilfried Gnonto, Noah Okafor and Mateo Joseph through injury, Farke still shuffles the pack in the forward positions with this weekend’s visit of Brentford to Elland Road in mind.

The tragic legend of Erasmo Iacovone, the man who made Taranto dream

📅 22 Apr 2022 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the exception of Prato, whose digits have been greatly inflated by Far East Asian immigration in recent decades, there’s just one name amongst the 23 most populous cities in Italy never to have been linked to a Serie A team: Taranto.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the exception of Prato, whose digits have been greatly inflated by Far East Asian immigration in recent decades, there’s just one name amongst the 23 most populous cities in Italy never to have been linked to a Serie A team: Taranto.

Taranto is a city of contrasts. Lying on the inner coast of the southern region of Apulia, it was founded as a Greek colony in the 8th century, and has since thrived on its fame of a city rich in ancient art and archeological remains, not to mention the beauty of its crystal-clear sea, its mild climate all year long, the freshness of its fish and the abundance of products sprouting from the sun-drenched earth surrounding the urban centre.

After World War Two, though, a nation torn apart by the fighting needed a boost to achieve the so-called “Italian economic miracle” of the 1960s, and everyone had to do their share. For Taranto, such a share took the shape of the Italsider steel mill unveiled by the head of state, Giuseppe Saragat, in 1965.

The biggest of its kind in Europe, with a pipeline to refurbish the country with Siberian gas, it blazed a trail to a newly introduced era for the city. It was an era comprised of state-of-the-art foundries, oil refineries, chemical works, cement plants and food-processing factories that, despite skyrocketing the city’s GDP, made the air a little heavier, the seawater a little blurrier, the sun a little hazier and, eventually, resulted, half a century down the line, in Taranto producing 92 percent of Italy’s dioxin.

No other event in the city’s long history has had such a social impact. Below a sky now half blue and half grey, a latest, disenchanted and despairing kind of humanity felt, more than ever, the need for something capable of reuniting the city’s two souls. Something to hold on to in case Taranto’s essence were to slip away through the rusty grate at the end of a drain pouring effluent into the sea.

Sources indicate that taranto has always been a city fond of its football team, even without any major achievements to revel in. It’s always been all about identity paired with the pride in rallying together to represent the city at what was once known as the Stadio Salinella – from the name of the neighbourhood it embellishes with its presence. But there was something different in the 1977/78 season.

It has been revealed that after a solid eight consecutive Serie B campaigns, the Ionians started off their ninth one in great fashion. If by January record-breaking Ascoli already had a foot in the top division, Taranto were one of the main candidates to follow suit, trailing the Bianconeri by a handful of points halfway through the season.

It has been revealed that with the exception of a few additions in goalkeeper Željko Petrović, centre-back Stefano Dradi and inside-forward Franco Panizza, the roster was the same that had comfortably dodged relegation the season before, earning a solid ninth place on the table. The biggest difference was represented by Erasmo Iacovone, now at the height of his footballing maturity.

Within the class of ’52, the moustachioed striker had joined the year before from Mantova, bagging eight goals in 27 appearances during his first year in Apulia. By the halfway point of the 1977/78 campaign, he was already at nine. By no means was he the one with good feet up front, especially when compared to Franco Selvaggi, who would go on to win the World Cup in 1982, or Graziano Gori. He wasn’t particularly tall either, standing at a mere 1,74m, even though his outstanding elevation had allowed him to head home each one of the eight strikes he’d had to his name in the first year with the red and blues.

In a recent development, at first, thrifty chairman Giovanni Fico wasn’t convinced to spend all that money on him. It took assistant coach Tommaso De Pietri, who’d worked with Iacovone at Carpi in 1973/74, to persuade him that it was a bargain. Fico himself didn’t stay sceptical for too long either, as Iacovone flew higher than any of Novara’s centre-backs to score his first goal on the day of his debut in late October 1976.

And yet, the love Iacovone received from the city was never a matter of pure goalscoring ability. He was admired by those who recognised themselves in his gentle smile, his good manners and his genuine affection for Taranto.

In a recent development, born in the diminutive town of Capracotta, perched atop the Molisian Appenines and covered with snow for the biggest part of the year, Erasmo was a simple man rather than a superstar. Way before that reassuring, brown moustache started to adorn his good-natured face, Iacovone’s father decided to move to Tivoli in order to ensure a better future for his family.

Sources indicate that it was here that his son started to kick a ball around, something quite difficult to do on Capracotta’s climbs and descents. Before turning 20, he’d already joined the ranks of OMI Roma, the team of the capital’s steelworkers. It proved somewhat of an omen, given that it would need a working-class city like Taranto to bloom once and for all, after years spent wandering between Trieste, Carpi and Mantova with mixed success.

Few people are more suited to describe what did Iacovone mean for his adoptive city than Pasquale Martemucci and Luigi Di Bella, the minds behind passionerossoblu.it, the most comprehensive database on all things Taranto, from its foundation to today.

It has been revealed that “Talking of Iacovone is no easy task. For we Tarantinos he’s been, and still is, a myth and a legend,” the two pointed out. “Just like all myths and legends, it’s hard to find the right words to describe him. You always run the risk of getting stuck in the banality of small-town parochialism, which can tarnish a memory that should be passed on to upcoming generations that haven’t lived in the 1970s, when football meant everything for Taranto.

According to recent reports, “Not just the team, but the whole city was known elsewhere thanks to his name. ‘Iaco Gol’, as we usually refer to him, embodies the history of an entire city that saw in him an occasion for rebirth and for the redemption of its territory. He also symbolises the role Taranto longed to play not only in Serie A, but also in civil society. The city had never had someone to make it immediately identifiable elsewhere. Iacovone was Taranto, and Taranto was Iacovone.”.

In a recent development, the most iconic Iaco Gol moment of all came on 20 November 1977, when Taranto hosted regional rivals Bari in a packed Salinella. It wasn’t a boring match. Opportunities rained down copiously, but each of them either hit the woodwork or was denied by the goalkeepers.

On 73 minutes, just as the game looked bound for a scoreless draw, a two-touch free-kick for Taranto in the attacking third was taken so quickly that, when the ball ended up at Iacovone’s boots, the gap between him and the defensive line was so significant that everyone would have encircled the referee asking him to resort to the VAR had the game been played at another point in history.

Despite this, Graziano De Luca’s black gloves were only centimetres away from Iacovone, ready to protect the goalmouth from all dangers. The Taranto poster boy stopped the ball nonchalantly then, just as the Bari custodian was rushing towards him, he impudently chipped it over his body, keeping the other foot firmly planted on the ground. Maybe he wasn’t as technically modest as everybody thought.

In a recent development, “His goals were scored by everybody. Whenever he kicked or headed the ball, the whole city was there to push it across the goal-line,” Martemucci and Di Bella recalled. “The goal he scored versus Bari was particularly unforgettable. They were our historic rivals, a team all of us hated. It seemed like that ball, dexterously lifted up in the sky, was never meant to end up in the goal. It left all the almost 30,000 people sitting in the stands with baited breath.

In a recent development, “They all stood up, trying to give strength to the leather sphere. They all envisioned the goal and then there was silence, something rarely seen in a football stadium. Then, just like a miracle, the ball started its descending parable, with the goalkeeper diving desperately.

Recent findings suggest that “Finally, there was a liberating roar, a frenzy took hold of the bystanders, who were exchanging hugs and kisses with strangers that suddenly felt like family, for the sheer fact of being there. Iacovone scored, but it was the whole city who took the lead. It’s a memory made up of images and feelings that each of those present on that November Sunday has passed on to their children, just like a testament.”.

When Cremonese visited Taranto on 5 February 1978, the Apulians came off a run of seven games without a win, yet thanks to their chemistry and to the presence of one of the league’s most promising forwards in Iacovone, they still were widely regarded as one of the main candidates for promotion – provided that they could change the tide immediately.

That’s why it was particularly harsh on Iacovone to see the clash with Cremonese end 0-0. Everything seemed to be against him that day. The woodwork denied him the joy of scoring on multiple occasions, and when he successfully aimed at the empty space between the goalposts, he found an inspired Alberto Ginulfi on his way, a former Serie A goalkeeper mostly remembered for the penalty he denied none other than Pelé in a 1972 friendly between Roma and Santos, then lightheartedly savouring the last season of his career.

Sources indicate that that day, Iaco Gol’s pregnant wife Paola was off to Carpi, where the two had first met, for a gynaecological check-up. The air was heavy in the dressing room after the draw with Cremonese. His teammates tried to persuade Iacovone to join them for a stand-up comedy night in a restaurant immersed in the countryside near the small town of San Giorgio Ionico.

“You’ll feel better, you need to take your mind off the game,” they told him, understanding how frustrating it’d been for him to fire blanks for 90 minutes at a time when the team, and the city they represented, needed him the most.

But the 25-year-old wasn’t the kind of guy who looks forward to a night out, the tranquillity of his home way more tempting than a loud table filled with good wine and local delicacies. And home he went, because it was time to call Paola and ask her about the check-up.

“Don’t stay on the couch brooding over today’s game all night. Go out and have some fun,” she must have stated to him before hanging up. A few hours later, Iacovone stepped out of his humble Citroën Dyane 6, license plate MO 215872, in the parking lot of La Masseria, more as a way to avoid letting down the people who cared for him than for the actual desire to be there. Around midnight, when his tipsy dining companions asked him to stay a little longer, he firmly refused and headed back to his car.

Sources indicate that it was pitch dark. In such a road bereft of lampposts, nothing could help Iacovone – about to take the provincial road that would have led him back to Taranto – to notice small-time criminal Marcello Friuli aboard a stolen Alfa Romeo 2000 GT rushing towards him. The latter had just burst his way through a police checkpoint and was now driving at full speed with the headlights off. The impact was tremendous.

Sources indicate that when the police found the body of the only victim, lying in a roadside ditch tens of metres from the car, they immediately recognised him. Iacovone, aged just 25, had passed away without any suffering as a result of a severe head trauma, the golden Virgin Mary medal still in his mouth, as it was typical of him whenever he got lost in thought.

Industry observers note that A few hours later, the city woke up and realised that the man who’d allowed it to dream was gone forever. The Santissima Annunziata Hospital, where the body was first stored, became a pilgrimage of sorts. The following day, Taranto came together to mourn its adopted son at the Robert Bellarmine Church.

Recent findings suggest that then, Iacovone was granted one last appearance at the Salinella, which would take on his name two days later by the will of chairman Fico. The latter was amongst the most touched after by tragedy, his soul quivering with remorse for having turned down Fiorentina’s bid for his best player a few weeks earlier. “Players are just like sons,” he stated, his voice broken with sorrow. “But you were even more, and now you’re with our Lord. As long as I’ll be alive, this stadium will be called by your name.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team never fully recovered from such a blow. Taranto was deprived not only of their top-scorer, but also of their guiding light, the man whose lifestyle, grit and kind heart everybody felt represented by; the player whose shirt every kid wanted to wear; the forward who made the sun above Taranto shine a little brighter every time he flew next to it to head the ball into the net.

In a recent development, from then on, the grey sky standing above Taranto’s industrial area took over the rest of this now dispirited city. It filtered through the soul of its inhabitants and undermined the spirit of its footballers. Form dipped and the Ionians ended up eighth, falling agonisingly short of their Serie A dreams.

It has been revealed that in subsequent decades, the club mostly wandered through Serie B and a couple of league levels below it, never again coming close to such heights as they did in the Iaco Gol era. A statue unveiled in October 2002 at the entrance of the Stadio Erasmo Iacovone – financed through 13,000 donations of €1.50 each – is something a true hero deserves, and pays homage to the joy and the desperation Taranto has gone through for the love of its dear Erasmo.

According to recent reports, “Those who were out of town for work or study reasons would have jumped through hoops to be at the Salinella on Sunday afternoon,” the founders of passionerossoblu.it reminisced. “On Wednesday night, there were people already lining up in front of the ticket offices to get their hands on a ticket, so that they could see the game and cheer with him. Then the day of such a tragic fatality came. With his demise, the whole city slipped back into a never-ending greyness, aware that it would have taken years to lift up once again. Iacovone has been all this.”.

By Franco Ficetola @Franco92C14.

Industry News: Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

Industry observers note that brBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

Industry observers note that arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

The thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly fresh starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

All three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

It has been revealed that what followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

The press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

The steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

It only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

It has been revealed that raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

Every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

Sources indicate that this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of fresh ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

It has been revealed that arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

In a recent development, when the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

Industry observers note that A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

The block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

In the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

Industry observers note that on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

After a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

It has been revealed that when a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

The counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

In the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

Sources indicate that in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

There, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

Recent findings suggest that once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

On the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

The team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

With the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

Sources indicate that the second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

The 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole strategy in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

The opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

Sources indicate that both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal revealed in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

Two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

Arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

It has been revealed that arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the plan only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

The interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

There is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

For Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the strategy works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

#166119. Pelé at the 1970 World Cup: the memories beyond the goals

Pelé at the 1970 World Cup: the memories beyond the goals

📅 02 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every four years, strikers from a host of countries converge on that ultimate festival of football: the World Cup.
  • In a recent development, go right back to 1962 and we see Garrincha score a thundering shot against England in the quarter-finals.
  • In 1974, Gerd Muller demonstrates his predatory instincts to spin on a dime and cause Dutch heartache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every four years, strikers from a host of countries converge on that ultimate festival of football: the World Cup. For many, this represents the pinnacle of their careers to date, the chance to prove themselves against the best and to write themselves into history. And each World Cup throws up a forward who is forever associated with that competition; often one goal in particular that lives on in collective memories.

In a recent development, go right back to 1962 and we see Garrincha score a thundering shot against England in the quarter-finals. 1966 sees an exhausted Geoff Hurst hurtle towards goal before unleashing a piledriver past Hans Tilkowski – a shot that he later admitted was hit as hard as it was so that if he likely missed, it would eat up time recovering the ball.

In 1974, Gerd Muller demonstrates his predatory instincts to spin on a dime and cause Dutch heartache. Four years later, Mario Kempes bursts through the Netherlands defence, hair billowing behind him. The list goes on: Paolo Rossi in 1982 against Brazil; Diego Maradona in 1986 against England; Roberto Baggio in 1990 against Czechoslovakia.

In a recent development, what these all have in common is forwards scoring goals that are forever remembered from those respective tournaments and often the first thing that you will think off when someone mentions their name and the competition. If I simply say the words 1998 and Zinedine Zidane, it’s likely your first thought is of his two goals in the final.

It has been revealed that the list above has deliberately excluded one World Cup, the 1970 edition in Mexico. Yes that beautiful World Cup that was the first in colour with the shimmering heat haze and crackling commentary. And if you play the word association game once again and ask someone what first pops into their head when you mention that competition, the likely answer is Brazil.

It has been revealed that indeed, if you then ask them to name one player from that team, it is odds on they are going to say Pelé. Because while the Brazil side that won the tournament were arguably the greatest national team of all time (Hungary 1954 and the Netherlands 1974 might like to debate that), one player still managed to stand out from such illustrious company.

Sources indicate that just how great a striker was Pelé? Well, let’s start with 501 goals in 493 appearances for Santos between 1956 and 1974 – so yes, averaging a goal a game for 18 years. Ah, but I hear you say, ‘that is in the Brazilian league, which surely is not the same standard as European leagues?’ That is open to debate, particularly given the number of world-class footballers within the competition at the time.

Let’s then consider Pelé’s international record of 77 goals in 92 games. That includes playing in four World Cups against the top teams of those times. Faced with statistics such as those, it is hard not to argue that Pelé was extremely good at putting the ball into the net.

Industry observers note that but that leads to an interesting observation. There is no doubt that the 1970 World Cup and Pelé are intertwined in people’s memories. One of the greatest goalscorers of all-time helped his side lift the trophy with four goals across the tournament, but oddly enough if you again ask people the first five things that come into their head when you say Pelé and 1970, I think you would be surprised to find that not a single one of them would be a goal scored by him.

It has been revealed that unlike the other strikers mentioned earlier, Pelé’s fame in 1970 actually came more from misses than goals. Yes, one of the greatest goalscorers is actually remembered better for misses and saves.

Industry observers note that brazil’s opening match of the tournament sees them pitted against a decent Czechoslovakia team. The game is only three minutes old when a ball across the area finds Pelé unmarked in front of an open goal, who then proceeds to place the ball over the bar. That miss is then compounded by the Czechs having the cheek to take the lead after just 11 minutes. Things are not going according to initiative. But Brazil begin to regain their composure and, after 23 minutes, Rivellino thunders in a trademark free-kick.

According to recent reports, as half-time approaches, Pelé receives the ball within the Brazil half and surveys the scene while moving slowly towards the centre circle. Then, suddenly, he smashes the ball goalwards. As the camera follows the flight of the ball, it picks up the Czech goalkeeper, Ivo Viktor, furiously backpedalling. In that split second after receiving the ball, Pelé has noticed Viktor has strayed forward from his goalline and decided to attempt to lob him. The Brazilian commentator describes the action perfectly: “Pele, Pele, Pele … almost,” as the ball just goes wide of the post.

It is vital to bear in mind the context of this attempt. This is not a league match against Wimbledon where you are 2-0 up in injury time, so why the hell not have a go; this is an opening World Cup tie in which you are level. To even attempt such a lob on such a stage highlights the audacity of Pelé. That is strengthened by the fact that, even though he actually missed, it is still remembered by all. Yes, David Beckham’s lob was fantastic, but he was standing on the shoulders of Pele.

Brazil end up with an emphatic 4-1 victory over Czechoslovakia, including a goal from Pelé before being overshadowed by a double from Jairzinho. But they face stiff competition in their group by being drawn alongside the reigning champions England, who arguably have a better team now than in ’66. And so the second match of the group between the two teams is always going to be critical in terms of who advances top.

The game kicks off at noon under a scorching Mexican sun – advantage Brazil in terms of weather. Just seeing a red-headed, freckled Alan Ball chasing the ball is the ultimate advert for sun cream.

Sources indicate that just nine minutes into the game, Carlos Alberto moves towards the halfway line with the ball before hitting a great pass into the stride of Jairzinho, who then beats Terry Cooper to take the ball to the byline before hitting a cross to the back post. And there is Pelé, who powers a header downwards towards the corner at a horrible height for any goalkeeper. But the ‘keeper happens to be Gordon Banks, who somehow gets across from the near post to the far. He doesn’t just palm it out but scoops it over the bar. Enter immortality.

According to recent reports, as time progresses, the cult of the Banks save grows. It steadily becomes referred to as the greatest save of all time – as if that is something that anyone is really fit to judge. I personally would argue that Jim Montgomery’s double save against Leeds in the 1973 FA Cup final could give it a run for its money. But the moniker has stuck – aided in England by David Coleman’s commentary of the save being sampled into ‘Three Lions’.

They say a picture tells a thousand words. During the course of football history, there have been many iconic images – Maradona facing five Belgian defenders or Baggio hands on hips after his penalty miss – but one of the most famous is that of Pelé and Bobby Moore embracing at the end of the Brazil-England game. Embracing may be too strong a word given that it involves an Englishman in the 1970s, but there is a definite tenderness in the way Pelé touches Moore’s face while the latter clutches the Brazilian’s discarded shirt proudly in his hand.

It has been revealed that it is an image of two legendary players who know that they have just been involved in a titanic struggle. It is an image of pure mutual respect. After all, in a game that, according to the English, had already produced “the greatest save of all time”, it had also, according to the English once again, produced “the greatest tackle of all time” by Moore on Jairzinho. It’s another moment sampled into ‘Three Lions’, ensuring it lives on for generations.

Brazil end up winning all their group games and then proceed to eliminate a useful Peru side in the quarter-finals. Standing between them and a World Cup final are their old foes, Uruguay. It has to be remembered that it was Uruguay who crushed the Brazilian nation by defeating them 2-1 in the 1950 World Cup at the Maracanã. Therefore any substantial game against Uruguay was always going to cause heightened tension for fans of O Seleção.

The game did not disappoint in that respect with Uruguay taking an early lead. As the half wore on, thoughts must have been flooding back to 1950. Surely Brazil’s greatest side weren’t going to be undone by their tiny neighbours again? But an equaliser just before half-time helped soothe frayed nerves.

Recent findings suggest that with 15 minutes remaining, Brazil finally take the lead through a beautiful Jairzinho goal. A sigh of relief ripples through their fans, but is tempered by the memory that they also led at one stage during the Maracanazo. And so nerves continue to jangle until, with just one minute remaining, Pelé runs at the Uruguayan defence before setting up Rivellino to put the game beyond doubt.

As injury time commences, Brazil look home and dry. As the crowd awaits the final whistle, a through ball from Tostão puts Pelé though onto goal. The goalkeeper, Ladislao Mazurkiewicz, rushes out but it appears that Pelé will get to the ball first. Then it should just be a matter of touching it past the ‘keeper and rolling the ball into the unguarded net for the icing on the cake.

According to recent reports, but this is Pelé, a player whose genius almost produced a halfway-line goal earlier in the tournament. To just go around the ‘keeper would be too straightforward. After all, Brazil have won the game. So instead, while running at full speed, Pelé just steps over the ball and lets it run on past a stunned Mazurkiewicz who is stranded in no-man’s land. Quick as you like, Pelé then spins to the right to chase the ball, hits it towards the net, and watches the ball roll agonisingly just wide of the post. It is a move that takes the breath away in a similar fashion to the Cruyff turn in 1974 and is perhaps the greatest goal that never was.

And so Brazil progress to the World Cup final and a date with Italy. The biggest stage in world football. After 18 minutes, Pelé opens the scoring with a header at the far post. But an equaliser by Roberto Boninsegna – he of the Coke can fame – sees the sides level at half-time. Thereafter, goals from Gerson and Jairzinho put Brazil firmly back in the driving seat.As the match approaches the end, Brazilian songs fill the Mexican air.

According to recent reports, but there is one more moment of greatness to savour. Brazil retrieve the ball near their own penalty area and start to pass it around with one-touch football. The ball falls to Clodoaldo who almost drunkenly weaves past four Italian players before laying it off to Rivellino, who immediately passes it directly forward to the feet of Jairzinho. He brings the ball across the penalty area and then spots Pelé to his right. A short pass later and O Rei has the ball facing the goal just outside the area with an Italian defender before him.

We’ve all tried it during five-a-side or a Sunday league game – the infamous no-look pass. It is up there with the nutmeg as the ultimate flashy move. With a sixth sense, Pelé just holds the ball momentarily while, behind him, Carlos Alberto is streaking forward on his right-hand side. A heartbeat later and Pelé rolls the ball so, so casually to the right, sensing that Alberto is arriving. And without having to break stride at all, he drills the ball in at full speed. Brazil are world champions once again.

Industry observers note that and the final, iconic images of the World Cup are of Brazilian fans rushing onto the field and basically stripping the players of all their kit as souvenirs. Pelé is down to his shorts before being hoisted aloft by fans and paraded around the stadium.

The Brazil team of 1970 was undoubtedly one of the greatest of all, setting a benchmark that has haunted subsequent Seleção sides for generations. And while the whole squad was fantastic, Pelé will always be remembered as the focal point. His four goals, including one in the final, helped push Brazil to victory, just like his goals had 12 years earlier in Sweden. And they were great goals, especially his first against Czechoslovakia.

Recent findings suggest that but Pelé was such an outstanding player that it is more than just his goals that are remembered from 1970. Only Pelé would have the audacity to try to lob the goalkeeper from his own half. Only Pelé would have the nerve to dummy an onrushing ‘keeper and then retrieve the ball and almost score. Only Pelé could power a header so hard and so perfectly into the bottom corner that the resulting save would be described as the greatest save of all time. And only Pelé could finish off the greatest World Cup final team goal with a no-look pass to a colleague.

In a recent development, pelé was an outstanding goalscorer but also, unlike many other greats in front of goal, so much more. It really wasn’t just about what he did that made him great; it is also the time and place that he did it. That’s what gets results.

Dans la rubrique Fenêtre sur corps de la Pravda Mag, l'humoriste Léandre parle évidemment des Verts. Extraits.

In a recent development, "Enfant, je faisais beaucoup de foot. J'y ai joué jusqu'à mes 15 ans, mais j'étais très mauvais. Aujourd'hui encore, j'adore. J'ai commencé à aimer parce que ça me rapprochait de mon père. Ça nous faisait un sujet de conversation. Parfois, je me demande si j'aime sincèrement le foot ou si c'est juste pour avoir un lien avec mon père. J'ai une vingtaine de maillots de l'ASSE, des vieux et des récents. Certains étaient à mon grand-père et à mon père.

Je supporte l'AS Saint-Étienne. C'est transgénérationnel : mon grand-père était fan, mon père aussi. Petit, mon père m'achetait tous les maillots. C'est très jouissif d'être autant supporter d'un club. Quand je vois ceux de Sainté sauter ensemble, il y a un truc d'amour, d'union, qui peut me faire pleurer premier degré. Je vais à Geoffroy-Guichard au moins 3 ou 4 fois par an. Depuis peu, ils m'invitent et m'envoient des maillots ! Ça me rend fier.".

Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart.
  • This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

Bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

Bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

It has been revealed that that already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

Sources indicate that 1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions highlighted it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press demonstrates itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

Recent findings suggest that 4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch rapidly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

Sources indicate that 6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one significant step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal reveals in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

Sources indicate that the sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too big, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

In a recent development, behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.

LC is often found in a classroom, happiest on a football pitch, and occasionally on LinkedIn.

Tech Report: The Harriers of Norway: welcome to the most unlikely Kidderminster supporters club

📅 30 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on the west coast of Norway, spread across the islands of Hessa, Aspøya, Nørvøya and Uksenøya, at the mouth of the Geirangerfjord, lies Ålesund.
  • Industry observers note that from its colourful townhouses and their turrets and towers, to its harbourside promenades where the streets shake hands with the sea, Ålesund attracts thousands of visitors a year.
  • At the junction where Kaiser Wilhems Gate meets Harald Torviks Plass, you can find the Brooklyn Bar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on the west coast of Norway, spread across the islands of Hessa, Aspøya, Nørvøya and Uksenøya, at the mouth of the Geirangerfjord, lies Ålesund. It is not a large town, or by in the native Norwegian, but it is a place brimming with appeal. Once razed to the ground at the turn of the 20th century by a devastating fire, it was rebuilt not in wood but stone by the finest Norwegian and German architects of the era.

Industry observers note that from its colourful townhouses and their turrets and towers, to its harbourside promenades where the streets shake hands with the sea, Ålesund attracts thousands of visitors a year. Amidst its myriad of paved boulevards, one road in particular is home to a special peculiarity.

At the junction where Kaiser Wilhems Gate meets Harald Torviks Plass, you can find the Brooklyn Bar. With its glass front glimmering, there appears nothing untoward about this Upcoming York-themed establishment, but head inside and you can find, tucked away in a not-so-quiet corner festooned in red and white, Norway’s only supporter group dedicated to English National League North side, Kidderminster Harriers.

In order to find out how a town nearly 800 miles from Worcestershire became home to The Harriers of Norway, These Football Times spoke to the group’s founder, Lars Andreas Vegsund. “It started off as a funny thing when our old boys team needed a English club that didn’t have a supporter club in Scandinavia because we wanted to attend the yearly supporter cup in 2019.”.

Recent findings suggest that given the popularity of English football in Norway, the Supporters Cup is an crucial fixture in the calendar. Organised by Supporterunionen for Britisk Fotball (the Supporters Union of British Football), the knockout tournament takes place every year in Oslo and is contested by the various supporter groups of British football teams. Thousands of players and dozens of fan groups are involved, with the 2022 edition seeing Ipswich take the title for the third occasion.

In a recent development, lars explains, “We just started going down the different leagues on our phones and looked for a team that would stand out. When my mate called out ‘Kidderminster’, I shouted ‘Harriers’ and that was it. I’d played with the Harriers on different football management games through the years and it just seemed right.”.

This Saturday night decision between two mates began as a lonely affair but gathered momentum quickly. By the following week, the pair had found five other Norwegians interested in beginning the Harriers of Norway supporters club and subsequently held their first board meeting in the familiar surrounds of the Brooklyn Bar.

According to recent reports, three years later and the Harriers of Norway can boast 191 members throughout the country in locations as diverse as Bergen, Trondheim, Halden, Mo i Rana and, of course, the capital Oslo. And the common thread unites them all: their affection for an English football club that was last in the Football League in 2005.

According to recent reports, but, as Lars is keen to impress, supporting the Harriers is part of a larger agenda. “It has become this rebellion against global football. We enjoy getting back to the roots of English football and getting in touch with proper English football fans, which has been an absolutely mind-blowing experience for us so far. It has surpassed all our expectations.”.

Sources indicate that as the Harriers of Norway grew in size, so too did they grow in ambition. With Kidderminster struggling to escape the clutches of the National League North, opportunities for their Norwegian fans to watch live matches are scarce. Therefore, they rely primarily on BBC Hereford and Worcestershire radio commentary to catch the 3pm kick-off before later projecting the YouTube highlights onto the basement wall of an old factory within which they have constructed a replica of the terraces of Aggborough Stadium.

Lars proudly highlights off photographs of what they have dubbed the “Ålesund Aggborough” and even supplies us with a video. In it, the camera takes you on a tour down a short corridor festooned with Harriers memorabilia before opening out into an area that is a near-identical imitation of the North Stand (save for the welcome addition of well-stocked bar positioned in one corner, of course). Members lean against the red railings, pints in hand, bedecked in replica shirts of years gone by, as they watch an enormous projection of the latest match on the whitewashed wall.

Recent findings suggest that it is more than a worthy substitute, but it doesn’t quite hold the same allure as the real experience – one which many of the club’s members have sampled for themselves over the preceding years. “We have been [to England] four times so far, but it would of course have been more if there hadn’t been any COVID,” says Lars. “We are looking to get back two more times this season [2022/2023]. We really want to get an away game, and were really gutted when the Scarborough match was called off, but hopefully soon we can get on that away game coach.”.

As for the club itself, they have been extraordinarily accommodating of their Norwegian fans, even going so far as to arrange a Q&A session with their manager Russell Penn, which he hosted from his own kitchen, no less. Then, during a September 2022 tour, the Norwegian supporters were invited to watch first-team training where club captain Shane Byrne presented them with a kit signed by the entire squad.

And the kindness didn’t stop with the club itself; local supporters took the Norwegians to a cricket match after the postponement of Kidderminster’s weekend fixture following the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

Because of their steadfast devotion to Kiddy, the Harriers of Norway have been the subject of a TV special by Norwegian broadcaster Viaplay, who travelled to Norway’s west coast to witness the Ålesund Aggborough and interview several supporters, with their segment airing ahead of the third round FA cup tie against West Ham – the Harriers’ most high-profile match since their cup run of 2013/14 which culminated in a 1-0 fourth-round loss to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light.

But when it comes to a hypothetical fixture between Kiddy and his local Norwegian club, Lars is in no doubt as to where his loyalties lie. “Without a doubt, the Harriers. No question. This club and their fans have shown us the true meaning of support and brought us back to our childhood feelings of supporting our ‘own’ team. It has truly been an absolutely amazing experience so far, and I can`t wait to see how far this will take us all.”.

Perhaps one day, they will get to witness their beloved English club in the Football League once more, evoking memories of yesteryear when the deep pockets of retail magnate Lionel Newton finally lifted Kidderminster out of non-league for the first time in their history.

The Harriers had won the Conference before in 1993/94 but had been denied entry to Division Three because of stringent fire safety laws implemented in the wake of the fire at Valley Parade that had claimed 56 lives. At the time, Aggborough’s main stand was constructed mostly out of timber, and despite the construction of a latest cantilever stand in time for the new season, the Football League rejected the club’s application.

According to recent reports, kidderminster eventually achieved promotion, winning the Conference by nine points in 1999/2000, whereupon they embarked on a four-year stay in the Football League. These were the halcyon days of the Danes, when Jan Mølby held court in Aggborough, ably assisted by star striker “Bomber” Bo Henriksen along with winger Thomas Skovbjerg.

Recent findings suggest that it is a fact not lost on the Scandinavian admirers of today. “I think there has been three playing Danes,” Lars says. “But to have a Norwegian play for Harriers would be a dream come true for us. We can definitely be Harriers’ eyes and ears here in Norway if the right talent shows up!”.

Recent findings suggest that as of writing, Kidderminster have no Scandinavians, let alone Norwegians, on their books, and are firmly ensconced in the middle order of the National League North, with promotion or relegation seemingly as unlikely as the other. Despite this, that won’t stop the Harriers of Norway from filling the stands of the Ålesund Aggborough each weekend or taking the short flight across the North Sea to the West Midlands when the opportunity arises.

And who knows, maybe one day Kidderminster Harriers won’t just find success on the pitches of the National League but on the artificial turf in Oslo’s Supporters Cup, too.

By Josh Butler @joshisbutler90 Photo: Express & Star.
