#166114. Bobby Robson, Ipswich Town and a brutal quest for the 1981 treble

📅 31 Jan 2023 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4221 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thesefootballtimes ↗ Open Full Page

Bobby Robson, Ipswich Town and a brutal quest for the 1981 treble

📅 31 Jan 2023 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter.
  • Sources indicate that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by.
  • But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wind blows hard and cold across East Anglia during the winter. With barely a hill in sight, there is nothing to stop the progress of the icy chill in this south east corner of England. An agricultural region, it is home to two principal football teams – Norwich City in Norfolk and Ipswich Town in Suffolk.

Sources indicate that while both teams are small in comparison to those from the major cities of England – London, Liverpool and Manchester for example – they’ve famously punched above their weight in times gone by. Norwich were particularly strong just after the Premier League began, finishing third in in the inaugural season before a famous UEFA Cup victory over the mighty Bayern Munich.

But overall, Ipswich have enjoyed more success, beginning with the appointment of Alf Ramsey as manager back in August 1955, when they were languishing in the Third Division (South) – a provincial team with no success to their name.

In a recent development, having played for England 32 times, including the infamous 1950 World Cup defeat to the US, Ramsey hung up his boots in 1955 and set about considering the next phase of his career. A player with a reputation for the tactical side of the game, it seemed natural that he would gravitate towards coaching. And so he was approached by the owners of Ipswich, the Cobbold Brewing family, to consider a player-manager role after their latest relegation to the third tier of English football.

Sources indicate that dismissing the playing role, he agreed to join them as manager at the age of 35. Everyone has to start somewhere, so while Ipswich were a small club languishing in the lower leagues, Ramsey was hoping it might be a stepping-stone to bigger things.

According to recent reports, no-one around Ipswich could possibly have dreamed about what would happen next. In his second season he secured promotion to the Second Division as champions with a team scoring over 100 goals, which was subsequently followed by a Second Division championship and promotion to the significant-time.

Incredibly, Ramsey then led Ipswich to become vhampions of England in their maiden campaign in the top-flight, an incredible achievement over the course of just four seasons. It was this amazing debut in management that led England to come knocking in 1963 – and the rest, as they say, is history.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, Ipswich didn’t build on this success and bumped between the First and Second tiers until the arrival of yet another future England managing great, Bobby Robson, in January 1969. Over the next decade, Robson built Ipswich into a successful side once again, the pinnacle being FA Cup glory in 1978 following a 1-0 victory over Arsenal, which could have been a much wider margin, such was Ipswich’s domination on the day.

It has been revealed that they were a regular top-five team over this period and a constant thorn in the side of more established teams such as Liverpool and Manchester United. This was personified in an incredible game during the 1979/80 season when Ipswich demolished Manchester United 6-0 at home despite the United goalkeeper saving two penalties. One question remained, however: could Robson take Ipswich one step further and convert a top five team into English champions against the mighty Liverpool?

It was against this backdrop that 1980/81 commenced. Ipswich had finished a strong third during the previous campaign, but behind both Manchester United and the dominant Liverpool team of the time. This was the Liverpool of Clemence, Neal, Hansen, Thompson, Case, Lee, McDermott, Souness and Dalglish. This was the Liverpool who not only won the title but also reached the semi-finals of both the League Cup and the FA Cup, managed by the legendary Bob Paisley. This was the Liverpool who dominated the late 1970s, having won four of the previous five campaigns. They were not going to give up their position of dominance lightly.

While the Liverpool squad sent shivers through all who met them, Robson had assembled a formidable squad of his own in his little corner of Suffolk. In goal was Paul Cooper, a keeper who joined Ipswich in 1974 and enjoyed a reputation as a penalty specialist. The defence included internationals such as George Burley, Terry Butcher, Mick Mills and Russell Osman. In fact, the England back line around that time often included Butcher, Mills and Osman, so good a defensive unit were they. But it was in midfield that things got especially interesting.

It has been revealed that in the 1970s, English football was still extremely insular. It was widely thought that foreign players were unable to cope with the rigors of English physicality and would wilt on a cold, rainy night in January. And really, who wanted all that fancy dribbling and passing that these continentals would bring over? English football was not a game for finesse.

According to recent reports, against this backdrop, Robson decided to buck the trend and go shopping overseas. In doing so, he brought in not one but two Dutch gems. The city of Enschede lies close to the German border and is home of FC Twente, and it is from there that Robson signed two midfielders in 1979, Arnold Muhren and Frans Thijssen.

In a recent development, the year before had seen Tottenham enjoy success with the double-signing of Ossie Ardiles and Ricky Villa, but the import of two non-British players was still a novelty at the time. The signing would prove to be a Robson masterstroke, bringing in two players with the ability to play the ball on the ground with an advanced level of skill.

He then just needed someone else in that midfield to provide a bit more “British grit”. Luckily exactly that player had joined Ipswich in 1975 to mature into one of the top players in England by 1980.

Sources indicate that to call John Wark combative is an understatement; he personified teamwork with energy that was second to none. Like Bryan Robson, he was a midfielder with the engine of a Rolls-Royce, who could run all day and shared the speciality of popping up in the area and scoring. For a midfielder, Wark had a phenomenal goalscoring record: he would end his Ipswich career with 94 goals from 266 appearances. And 1980/81 was going to see him in his prime.

Sources indicate that in attack, when Wark wasn’t dashing in to score, Eric Gates, Paul Mariner and Alan Brazil supplied plenty of firepower. Gates had played for Ipswich his whole career after making his debut at just 18 in 1973, with his finest moment coming when he netted both goals in a 2-1 win over Barcelona at Portman Road in the 1979 Cup Winners Cup quarter-final.

Mariner, meanwhile, had been a club-record signing from Plymouth for the princely fee of £220,000 and had established himself as an England target man under Ron Greenwood. Alan Brazil also enjoyed status as an international within Scotland.

Industry observers note that so going into the 1980/81 season, while their squad may not have been as deep as Liverpool, it was packed with established internationals from England, Scotland and the Netherlands. Providing the key players could keep injury-free, there was no reason why they couldn’t push on to new heights. They also had a UEFA cup campaign to look forward to.

It has been revealed that as they travelled to Leicester on the opening day, there was a cautious mood of optimism amongst the fans. That optimism was soon justified as Ipswich started the season in fine form. After winning the opener at Filbert Street, they proceeded to win seven of their first eight league fixtures. In the days of two points for a win, they opened up a four-point gap on Liverpool, Everton and a developing Aston Villa.

Wark was showing his uncanny goalscoring ability with six goals in those eight games as both Villa and Everton were defeated at Portman Road, the latter 4-0. But October would prove a more realistic test with trips to both Liverpool and Manchester United looming.

September also saw Ipswich begin their UEFA cup campaign, Wark again going on a scoring spree, netting four goals – including a hat-trick of penalties – at Portman Road against Aris Salonika, giving Ipswich a 5-1 victory which would be enough despite a 3-1 defeat back in Cyprus. A pattern would develop over the campaign of winning at home but losing away.

Back in the league, October saw Ipswich travel to Anfield and come away with a respectable draw thanks to a Thijssen goal. They followed that with another 1-1 draw at home to Manchester United. They had played the top two teams from the previous season and maintained their unbeaten record. The end of October did, however, see Aston Villa take the top spot, albeit only two points ahead of Ipswich who had two games in hands over the Villains.

It has been revealed that the end of October saw Ipswich’s next European adventure as, once again, a first leg win at home saw them establish a 3-0 win over Bohemians Prague, with Wark inevitably scoring twice, before another away leg scare that saw them lose 2-0 but hang on to progress to the third round. Wark now had six European goals to go along with his impressive domestic tally and seemed to be single-handedly dragging Ipswich along.

According to recent reports, it was game 15 of the season that finally saw Ipswich suffer their first defeat – and surprisingly it occurred away at basement-dwellers Brighton. But they immediately bounced back with back-to-back wins to finish November in third, behind Villa and Liverpool but still with three games in hand. The end of November also saw Portman Road again host a UEFA Cup first leg – against Widzew Lodz of Poland – on a night few would forget.

According to recent reports, widzew had impressively knocked out Manchester United and Juventus in the preceding two rounds and included a young striker who was getting quite the reputation by the name of Zbigniew Boniek. Juve decided to continue to monitor his progress, leading to his eventual signing and successful partnership with Michel Platini at the Delle Alpi.

But on this night in November, they would be swept aside 5-0 by Ipswich, inclusive of another Wark hat-trick. Of course, Ipswich then went on to lose the return leg in Poland 1-0, but the Portman Road faithful now truly believed. The European adventure was in full flight but would now be on hold until March. Until then, it was back to blustery cold Suffolk for a continued league campaign and the start of the FA Cup.

According to recent reports, december saw six league games including a home draw against Liverpool, a much-enjoyed home victory in the East Anglian derby over Norwich, and just one defeat away at Tottenham. By month’s end, Ipswich were just a single point behind leaders Liverpool and Villa, but still with two games in hand. Attention now turned to the FA Cup.

According to recent reports, the FA Cup still retained its magic back in the 80s with full-strength teams sent out, fan fever and budding romance. Ipswich had enjoyed a strong bond with the competition in recent times, winning it in 1978, and so it was with excitement that fans awaited the draw to see how their latest campaign would commence. The beauty of the open FA Cup draw delivered, throwing Ipswich a third-round tie at home against Aston Villa.

It has been revealed that unsurprisingly it would prove to be a tight game, but a moment of magic from the Dutch duo led to an early Mariner goal, which proved enough on the night. The reward was a fourth-round tie away at Second Division Shrewsbury.

Recent findings suggest that as evident in their UEFA Cup campaign, Ipswich had a poor track record away from home in the cups, and that continued at Gay Meadow as the Tractor Boys came away with a 0-0 draw in a game that Robson admitted they were lucky to have survived. Ipswich’s home form saw them win the replay 3-0 and set up a fifth-round tie in February at home to Charlton.

Ipswich’s January league campaign saw them win three and draw one, scoring 11 goals over the three games, a strong run that saw them return to the top of the table ahead of Aston Villa on goal difference and with champions Liverpool beginning to drop away. It was a stellar month that meant Ipswich were now top of Division One, in the fifth round of the FA Cup and in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Cup.

Industry observers note that february saw them build on this momentum as they won all four league games and beat Charlton 2-0 in the FA Cup, leaving them two points ahead of Villa in what was now effectively a head-to-head race and awaiting Nottingham Forest away in an FA Cup quarter-final. The whispers began around England: could Ipswich actually win the treble of league, FA Cup and UEFA Cup? Heady stuff, indeed.

There was one major obstacle ahead in terms of the treble. March saw Ipswich return to Europe, and the UEFA Cup draw had given them the toughest of ties: St-Etienne. Three-time league champions during the 1970s and European Cup runners-up in 1976, it was a squad that boasted the likes of Battiston, Lopez, Larius, Rep and a certain Platini.

This was the Platini who would soon be joining Boniek in Turin and who would win European Footballer of the Year in 1983, ’84 and ’85. It was a team with serious European pedigree – and Ipswich had to travel to the Stade Geoffery-Guichard first.

Industry observers note that it was a legendary night for the boys from Suffolk. Gates were closed two hours ahead of kick-off as 42,000 crammed into the stadium. It was 26 years since St-Etienne had last lost a European tie at home. An early headed goal from Dutch star Rep in the iconic green shirt had the crowd whipped into a frenzy as Ipswich’s poor away cup form continued. But then a powerful header from Mariner left the teams level at the half. And then the miracle occurred.

Just two minutes from the restart, some nice interplay from Ipswich saw Wark pass the ball to Muhren outside the area. Without hesitating, Muhren unleashed a left-foot screamer into the top corner, giving the goalkeeper no chance. Ipswich had their first UEFA Cup lead away from home.

With confidence surging, a ball out to Brazil on the right saw his cross volleyed by Butcher before Mariner swooped in to score Ipswich’s third. St-Etienne were on the ropes and the knockout blow came from who else but Wark with a strong header into the corner. Ipswich had ended their away curse in style. Robson commented: “We have demolished a good side with one of the best victories anyone has achieved in Europe in the past ten years.”.

As if to reinforce the point, Ipswich then comfortably won the return leg 3-1 in front of a packed Portman Road. Needless to say, Wark was on the scoresheet once again. Suddenly all of Europe was aware of the Tractor Boys.

In between these two historic games, they also travelled to Nottingham to take on Brian Clough’s Forest in the FA Cup quarter-final. A pulsating tie ensued as Forest literally gifted Ipswich a two-goal lead only to see it evaporate as Trevor Francis, Colin Walsh and John Robertson turned the game on its head.

Recent findings suggest that it seemed that finally the volume of games had caught up with Ipswich and the treble dream was crumbling. But then a shot by Thijssen took a cruel deflection and the blues escaped with a lucky draw. The replay was won 1-0 and the treble dream was back on … just. Ipswich were in the semi-finals of both the FA Cup and UEFA Cup.

Recent findings suggest that but all these games were beginning to drain a small squad and cracks finally began to show during March in their league form. After having lost two games all season, March saw them defeated in successive away games at Manchester United and Leeds. It was enough to still see Ipswich top at the end of the month, just a point ahead of Aston Villa. It was a first ominous sign.

Recent findings suggest that and so the season was coming towards the end with Ipswich entering April top of the league and in two major semi-finals. A historic treble was still in play – if Ipswich could just maintain their momentum through the final weeks. But they were facing eight games during April. With a skeleton squad, they were going to need a reserve of energy and a bout of luck to negotiate such a schedule.

The final nervewracking endgame commenced under the ultimate definition of fixture congestion, and the diary evolved as follows:.

Ipswich visit West Brom in the league and suffer their third successive away loss 3-1 – the irony being that West Brom’s victory helps their arch-rivals Aston Villa.

Ipswich face the first leg of their UEFA semi-final against a powerful Koln at Portman Road, boasting the likes of Littbarski, Bonhof and Dieter Muller. A full house sees Ipswich establish a slim 1-0 first-leg victory courtesy of a header from Wark.

Ipswich travel up to Villa Park for their FA Cup semi-final against Manchester City. A crowd of 46,000 watch a nervy game remain goalless before entering extra time with Beattie having an effort cleared off the line. Then a through ball to City’s Bennett sees him tussle with Butcher, with a free-kick somewhat harshly awarded to City around 30 yards from goal.

What happened next lives in Manchester City folklore; skipper Paul Power curls the free-kick past Cooper into the top corner. It leaves Ipswich with 20 minutes to rescue the treble dream, but it isn’t to be. It has taken three games in eight days to finally break them, but break them it has. The treble is no more.

Ipswich now have the titanic task of picking themselves up from defeat – and a 120-minute match – to revisit Villa Park just three days later for a possible league decider. After three successive away defeats, a loss here would virtually hand Villa the trophy.

Over 47,000 fans pack Villa Park for the title decider. A hopeful long ball sees Villa defender McNaught under no pressure, except that he fails to notice Mariner closing in behind him. Before he knows what is happening, Mariner pokes the ball from him and Brazil slots Ipswich into the lead. Suddenly the confidence is back and an early second-half Villa surge is thwarted twice by Cooper.

It has been revealed that villa once again go into self-destruct mode as a wayward pass from Bremner allows Mariner to play in Gates for a second Ipswich goal. Villa come back with a beauty from Gary Shaw but Ipswich hang on to rekindle their title hopes. In three days, Ipswich players go from despair to ecstasy on the same Villa Park turf.

Sources indicate that another league game as Ipswich host Arsenal at Portman Road. The endless matches are now taking their toll and Robson chooses to rest Thijssen while Kevin Beattie is absent with a broken arm. Unfortunately, Ipswich finally experience their first home loss of the season as Arsenal leave with a damaging 2-0 victory, with the opening goal initially disallowed for offside before a change of mind following a referee-linesman consultation. An injured Gates has to be substituted during the game to add to Ipswich’s injury woes.

Just two days after their first home defeat of the season, Ipswich must travel to Norwich for the East Anglian derby. If any team will delight in derailing Ipswich’s title push, it will be the Canaries. Almost 26,000 rabid Norwich fans pack Carrow Road to urge their team on. Despite being near the bottom of the table, they shock Ipswich by inflicting a 1-0 defeat. It seems now that the title is heading to Villa Park, much to the delight of those in yellow.

Again, a mere two-day rest and then off to Koln to defend their narrow 1-0 first-leg advantage. An insane schedule for any team but possibly the last leg of the treble still alive. But Ipswich again drag themselves off the canvas and win 1-0, courtesy of an unlikely goalscorer in Butcher, to reach the UEFA Cup final.

In a recent development, back to Portman Road for a must-win home tie against their FA Cup foes Manchester City. Butcher again becomes the hero as he scores the only goal of the game – and Ipswich are still just in the title race. Two games are left in May to decide the league with two UEFA final legs sandwiched in between against AZ Alkmaar.

With Aston Villa now almost over the finishing line, Ipswich travel to Middlesborough in a must-win game while Villa travel to Arsenal. Arsenal win 2-0 but play against a backdrop of singing Villa fans as the news circulates around Highbury that Ipswich are losing at Ayresome Park. The defeat means that the second part of the treble dream is officially over as Villa are crowned Division One champions. In the space of under a month, two legs of the stool have been removed. Only the UEFA Cup dream remains.

In a recent development, another short rest and then the first leg of the UEFA Cup final against AZ. Once again, Ipswich breathe life into tired legs as they run out 3-0 victors with goals from Wark, Thijssen and Mariner. A rocking Portman Road celebrates, but knowing their shaky away record, nothing is certain yet.

According to recent reports, finally – finally – Ipswich’s marathon season draws to a close as they travel to the Netherlands to secure European glory. A great start sees Thijssen score against his countrymen after just four minutes. Nerves start to jangle as AZ grab two goals in the next 21 minutes to go ahead before Wark, inevitably, returns calm with an equaliser. Undeterred AZ score again to take a 3-2 lead into the half-time break.

Then, on 73 minutes, they go 4-2 up, meaning an aggregate lead now of just 5-4 to Ipswich, but with away goals advantage., AZ still need a further two. But Ipswich hold out and finally one of the three trophies that they have been chasing all year is in their hands.

So, after a season that saw Ipswich play a staggering 66 games across four competitions, they finished as UEFA Cup champions, First Division runners-up and FA Cup semi-finalists. Overall, this represented an incredible achievement for the team from Suffolk with a limited squad and resources.

Robson had demonstrated his talent for developing talent while also integrating foreign flair, leading him to a great career spanning PSV, Barcelona, Newcastle, England and a knighthood.

It has been revealed that in a way, Ipswich were actually unlucky not to win the league given Liverpool were having a relative off-season (they still won the European Cup and League Cup but finished fifth in Division One). Unfortunately for the Tractor Boys, they came up against a once-in-a-lifetime Aston Villa team who had a much lighter schedule of matches.

Industry observers note that it is hard to imagine nowadays having to play eight highly competitive, stressful games in a month with a limited squad at the end of a long season – but that is what Ipswich faced. It is no wonder, then, that they failed to convert all three opportunities. The fact that they got as close as they did is achievement enough.

The 1980/81 season represented the apogee of that talented side. The following season would see them again end as Division One runners-up behind a rejuvenated Liverpool, but the UEFA Cup triumph would be their last major trophy up to the current day.

For all those fans who witnessed it, the 1980/81 season will live in their hearts forever. From humiliating Platini and co in France to a classic cup win over Clough’s Nottingham Forest and a snatch-and-grab win at Villa Park against the champions-to-be, many indelible memories were formed.

As for John Wark, he ended the season as the top scorer in the UEFA Cup with a staggering 14 goals in just 12 games. And then, just to rub it in further, he grabbed 18 Division One goals and two apiece in the League Cup and FA Cup. It took his total tally for the campaign to 36, ten ahead of the next best, Mariner. An Ipswich legend was born.

Recent findings suggest that the last word should go to the great man himself. Looking back on the season, the late Sir Bobby Robson stated, “People loved us and it was one of the few occasions where we actually made people sing. The ’81 team, in my opinion, was the best side [I managed]. We played the sort of football that hadn’t been seen in for many, many years … and not only just in Ipswich but I think in England.” If Sir Bobby thinks that, then who are we to argue?

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:30 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:03 EST, 23 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to buy Manchester United out of trouble in the January transfer window.

Pochettino admitted that United are in a relegation battle after a painful 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in his first game in charge left the club second from bottom of the Premier League.

Sources indicate that it’s understood the Argentine will have a limited budget well under £50million with United’s hands tied by the league’s latest financial rules. Pochettino is only expected to make two new signings in January, even if one of them is a loan deal.

Sources have not ruled out the possibility of United gambling if there is a genuine threat of the club being relegated for the first time in 53 years, but they would still have to spend responsibly.

The defeat to Liverpool underlined the need for Pochettino to strengthen in central defence, with Brentford’s Nathan Collins emerging as a strong candidate ahead of Calvin Bassey, who is expected to sign a new contract with Fulham, and Everton’s Jarrad Branthwaite who is valued at over £70million.

United also want a left-back after failing to sign cover for Luke Shaw in the summer when they were linked with Barcelona’s Alejandro Balde and Rayan Ait-Nouri of Manchester City. Both those players could be potential targets again.

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to try and fix Manchester United in January.

Pochettino is only expected to make two upcoming signings in January - pictured: Chief executive Omar Berrada (left) and director of football Jason Wilcox (centre).

Pochettino would also like a fresh striker after Benjamin Sesko’s shin injury left him short of firepower until the New Year.

Monaco’s Folarin Balogun, who played under Pochettino for the US national team, Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Ivan Toney, the former Brentford centre-forward now playing for Al-Ahli, have all been linked with a move to Old Trafford.

However, Toney’s £500,000-a-week wages put him out of United’s reach, and Leeds are keen to extend Calvert-Lewin’s contract which is worth £180,000-a-week.

Meanwhile, United are appealing to the FA over Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool.

Sources indicate that yoro was sent off in the eighth minute at Anfield for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free-kick.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

#166111. Breaking: The tale of Queen’s Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs

Breaking: The tale of Queen’s Park: the early innovators who became last of the amateurs

📅 06 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thesefootballtimes

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the year is 1872.
  • Industry observers note that meanwhile, on 30 November, the first international association football match to be retrospectively recognized by FIFA as “official” takes place at Hamilton Crescent, Glasgow, between Scotland and England.
  • According to recent reports, if someone says the word Glasgow to you, what images does it conjure up as a football fan?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the year is 1872. Ulysses S. Grant is elected president of the US, Yellowstone becomes the world’s first national park, and the first case of Horse Flu is reported in Toronto, Canada, which will substantially disrupt life in North America by mid-December.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, on 30 November, the first international association football match to be retrospectively recognized by FIFA as “official” takes place at Hamilton Crescent, Glasgow, between Scotland and England. And remarkably, the whole Scottish team is comprised of players from just one single club.

According to recent reports, if someone says the word Glasgow to you, what images does it conjure up as a football fan? I am guessing the Old Firm – Celtic vs Rangers, Green vs Blue, Catholic vs Protestant – the two historically strongest teams in Scotland involved in one of the world’s most passionate derbies. Two teams which, while sworn enemies, need each other to feed off, as seen during the recent years when Rangers’ absence from the top flight resulted in the loss of this great match-up.

What you might not be aware of, however, is that halfway between the famous theatres of Ibrox and Celtic Park, to the south, sits the 52,000-capacity Hampden Park, home of the national team, which was built in 1903 and was the biggest stadium in the world at the time.

In a recent development, hampden Park was in fact the third stadium built in the area under that name. The very first was initially used in October 1873 by the oldest club in Scottish football. That club wasn’t Celtic or Rangers but a team nicknamed The Spiders, who were formed way back in 1867, making them the oldest club in the world outside of England and Wales. That club is Queen’s Park.

According to recent reports, queen’s Park have an important role to play in the history and development of the modern game that we know and love. In those days, they dominated Scottish football. Indeed, the early playing rules in Scotland were developed at Queen’s Park. The were also the instigators of the Scottish Football Association and the first-ever winners of the Scottish Cup in 1874.

As mentioned, 1872 saw the maiden game between Scotland and England, the former fielding 11 players all from the same team: you guessed it, Queen’s Park. The game ended 0-0 and had the great claim that the two teams used the following formations: Scotland went 2-2-6 while England fielded a more attacking 1-1-8. How the game ended 0-0 with those formations is anyone’s guess.

Sources indicate that highlighted by such formations, early football tactics were pretty rudimentary. It often consisted of giving the ball to one player, who then rushed upfield surrounded by teammates in a battering ram formation more similar to what we now recognise as rugby. But yet again, Queen’s Park moved the game forward. It was there that a revolutionary upcoming tactic was invented. What if, instead of just charging with the ball until tackled, one passed the ball to a colleague when challenged?

This idea of combining together as a team, which led to the term “combination football”, helped Scottish football lead the way. Queen’s Park were the Barcelona of the 1870s, with this sharp, alien-like, movement of the ball. In March 1872, the Spiders were drawn to play against Wanderers in the FA Cup – Scottish teams took part in this famous competition until 1887 – and crushed them 5-0. A description of the game in the press included the following: “The play was now in the centre, the Queen’s Park men dribbling and passing, while their opponents indulged chiefly in heavy kicking.”.

Recent findings suggest that one can only imagine the stunned Englishmen watching on, monocles dropping in shock as their faces reddened beneath their handlebar moustaches. The gall of those bounders! Teamwork: what an outrageous proposition.

In a recent development, and so, from 1874 to 1893, Queen’s Park won ten Scottish Cups – still the third-highest total behind Celtic and Rangers – and even participated in two FA Cup finals, the only Scottish team to ever do so. They were probably the leading team across the Isles at the time, and therefore within the world.

So where did it go wrong for this club of innovators? Why did such a dominant force fade into the background? The answer to that lies in the next key development of the game: money.

When Queen’s Park were strutting their stuff and revolutionising the game, football was still a gentleman’s pastime dominated by players from public school backgrounds who played to enjoy camaraderie, healthy exercise and a few hearty drinks after. These players were usually professionals in other fields for whom football was just an amateur hobby on the side.

Early FA Cup competitions were won by teams such as Oxford University, Old Etonians and Old Carthusians – names dripping of cigar smoke, hallowed halls and back-slapping chums. But as competitions developed, the game spread into more working-class areas, especially in the north of England, until in 1983, the Old Etonians were shockingly defeated by one such outfit, Blackburn Olympic.

Long before Jack Walker and his steel money brought success to the industrial Lancashire town, Blackburn Olympic were formed. The town revolved around cotton, with mills employing thousands living a tough life fraught with danger and monotony. Football proved to be an attractive diversion and rose swiftly in popularity. However, the idea of a working-class team lifting the FA Cup was an anathema to the ex-public schoolboys that they concocted the Football Association. Surely some skullduggery must be behind such happenings.

The players of Blackburn Olympic were amateurs in that they all worked for local mills. But then again, did they truly “work” for these mills? For example, before the FA Cup final, the team had gone to Blackpool for several days of special training. But what were mill-workers doing missing several days of work? Were they still being paid during this trip? And who were these Scottish workers who played for the team? What had induced these talented footballers to leave their homeland and come south to work in a mill?

Industry observers note that the answer, of course, was that Blackburn Olympic were arranging “jobs” for their players and supplementing their income with additional payments. These included the Scottish players, known as the “Scotch Professors”, who brought down their passing game to many of the northern teams.

According to recent reports, and so as the northern teams began to dominate English football, tensions soon came to a head. Preston beat Upton Park in the FA Cup, who then protested against the presence of paid players in the Preston ranks. Debate raged until around 30 northern clubs threatened to break away from the FA if professionalism was not allowed. And so, in July 1885, the inevitable occurred and the professional era came into official existence.

It has been revealed that the Scottish FA, however, were having none of it. They withdrew their teams from the FA Cup in protest. Unsurprisingly, money spoke and a significant number of Scottish players relocated south of the border, to the extent that when Preston won the first-ever Football League in 1889, they fielded ten Scottish professionals.

Industry observers note that the Scottish Football League was launched in 1890 on an amateur basis, but Queen’s Park declined to join, on the supposition that, like in England, it would be a sham and not truly amateur. And so it proved. It didn’t take long for it to be obvious that clubs were accumulating talent through financial incentives. By 1893, Scotland too bowed to the inevitable and formalised professional football.

So what do you do if you are Queen’s Park – you are one of the innovators of the game and you believe in the amateur spirit – and see all around you paying for talent? The obvious answer is that, if you can’t beat them, join them. But this is where the story of Queen’s Park takes a remarkable twist. They decided to remain an amateur club while still playing within the Scottish League system. And they keep doing so for over 125 years.

Recent findings suggest that up until 2019, 126 years after Scotland approved professionalism, Queen’s Park stuck to their guns as an amateur outfit. Having been founded as the oldest club in Scotland, it meant they’d effectively been amateur for 152 years. Their pride in such included sporting the Latin motto Ludere Causa Ludendi (To Play for the Sake of Playing).

In a recent development, as the decades rolled by, maximum wages were introduced then abolished, The Bosman ruling was rendered and super-agents sent player wages into the stratosphere. Ashley Cole almost crashed his car when he heard Arsenal were only going to pay him a miserly £60,000 a week.

And still Queen’s Park held out as a final bastion of the amateur spirit, sticking to the Corinthian spirit. One almost pictures a team stuck in time, still patrolling the field in knickerbockers and finely waxed moustaches, whilst being overrun by youths in shiny, sponsored shirts. But there is a nobleness in their decision.

There was one downside to this noble stance, however: before 1893, Queen’s Park played in two FA Cup finals and won ten Scottish Cups; after 1893, they have won nothing except lower division titles.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, though, cracks appeared. In 1998, the club was stuck in the fourth tier of Scottish football. Something had to be done and so its constitution was amended to allow the signing of former professionals, providing that they still remained unpaid by Queen’s Park. Before that point in time, even ex-professionals were not permitted within Hampden Park. The manager, John McCormack, then stretched the interpretation of the fresh constitution to permit the loaning of professionals. And lo and behold, Queen’s Park went on to win the league and gain promotion in 2000.

Industry observers note that unfortunately this latest approach didn’t yield increased success for long. The next season saw Queen’s Park relegated again before then finishing bottom of the last tier the following year – the first time in their history that they sat at the base of Scottish football.

The 2012/13 campaign saw Queen’s Park joined by one of their substantial city neighbours, Rangers, following their fall into administration. And in April 2013, Rangers hosted Queen’s Park in front of almost 50,000 fans, setting a latest record for a crowd at fourth-tier level, who watched the 4-0 thumping dished out by the big boys.

Industry observers note that unsurprisingly, Rangers ran away with the title that year, while Queen’s Park made the playoffs but lost out to Peterhead. One member of that team was a young Andy Robertson, who wisely decided on accepting an offer to play for the Spiders rather than starting university, a decision that proved a wise choice in light of his subsequent career trajectory.

According to recent reports, up to this point, Queen’s Park still played their home games at the famous Hampden Park. The craziness of that situation was epitomised by Hampden having a capacity of almost 52,000 post-Taylor Report, while Queen’s Park’s average attendance was around 600-700 souls. One can only imagine the atmosphere within the vast cavernous ground as fewer than a thousand people packed together in a small group to cheer on their beloved club.

Industry observers note that but Queen’s Park still owned the famous ground, with a lease granted to the SFA expiring 2020. In 2018, a deal was agreed by which the SFA would purchase Hampden Park outright from Queen’s Park on expiry of the lease for £5m. Queen’s Park used some of those proceeds to develop their neighbouring training ground, known cutely as Lesser Hampden, into a 1,774-capacity stadium for home games. Having played their last game at Hampden in March 2021, they have ground-shared with Falkirk, Patrick Thistle and Stenhousemuir as they continue to develop Lesser Hampden.

With aims in place to downsize their stadium, and the threat of being overtaken by teams from the Highland and Lowland Leagues, the Spiders realised that their long-held model of amateurism was no longer feasible. And so in 2019, after 152 years of proud amateur status, Queen’s Park decided to vote on whether to become professional. If 75% percent of members voted in favour, they would finally be able to hire players on full-time contracts, fend off offers from competing teams, and receive compensation for players moving on.

The realisation that they were developing youth players who then just moved elsewhere upon turning 18 was becoming too much to bear. The motion was presented on 14 November 2019 and saw 91 percent of the members vote in favour. The last bastion of amateur football was felled.

In a recent development, emotions were understandably mixed. “The committee of the club plotted a course to try to defend ourselves against the threats of other ambitious clubs around us wishing to become a senior league club,” former Queen’s Park striker Crawley told BBC Scotland. “We are keen to arm ourselves to fend that off and progress. It was head against heart. The heart of a lot of the membership would be we really don’t want to do this, but we have to do it.”.

It has been revealed that the club’s official Twitter site thanked fans for their involvement, stating, “We recognise the difficulty in introducing this resolution. However, we believe this will enable us to plan for a bright future as we face up to the challenges of moving from the national stadium and maintaining our senior league place.”.

Was the move successful? Well, the 2019/20 season was ended early by the COVID-19 pandemic but the summer saw Queen’s Park use their new status to sign several professional players. And lo and behold, 2020/21 saw Queen’s Park promoted to the third tier as champions, a full 16 points ahead of second place Edinburgh City. And if that wasn’t enough, the 2021/22 season saw Queen’s Park promoted yet again through the Championship playoffs, defeating Airdrieonians over two legs.

As of today, Queen’s Park now sit atop the Scottish Championship, promotion from which would take them into the Premiership and back with the likes of their lofty neighbours, Celtic and Rangers.

In a recent development, there is a part of me that is sad to think that, in order to survive, Queen’s Park had to finally bow to modern pressures and lose their status as the only amateurs still standing. But despite this change, Queen’s Park still have an amazing legacy that they can proudly cling to.

According to recent reports, for their first five years of existence, they never conceded a goal. For their first seven years of existence, they never lost a game. They won the Scottish Cup ten times and even participated in two FA Cup finals. They are even credited with being the first team to play two halves of 45 minutes each with the novel concept of a half-time break, as well as introducing free-kicks, turnstiles and crossbars. Imagine a game of football without crossbars.

The Spiders came up with the heretic notion of passing the ball rather than just rushing it upfield – a notion which some teams still struggle with even today. They organised the first Scotland vs England game and fielded the entire Scottish team. And then they maintained their amateur ethos despite their last trophy of significance being the Scottish Cup in 1893.

It has been revealed that somewhere, a former Queen’s Park director is looking down from above. “Damn fine to see our boys getting back to where they belong. But playing for money, well that is just utter rot. Man should stretch his sinews for the pure love of the game itself.” And with that, he puffs on his oversized cigar, downs his 15-year-old single malt, and twiddles his beautifully waxed moustache.

It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest major-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his new club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

According to recent reports, “A perfect day for him,” said De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

Sources indicate that “We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”.

Industry observers note that "What an introduction!"Sávio scores a brilliant goal on his Spurs debut! 👏 pic.twitter.com/WgmcfgeNpX.

Having watched some of Tottenham’s signings fall to a 3-0 Premier League defeat by Brentford a few days earlier, Sávio’s late impact was the perfect lift for the Spurs supporters.

The club have committed to spending almost £400m this summer, leading to debate by outsiders over whether it will prove to be money well spent and huge waves of excitement within the fanbase.

A deal that could be worth as much as £85m, if add-ons are achieved, for Sávio certainly raised some eyebrows, but the Brazilian provided the perfect response by scoring just 11 minutes into his debut as a late substitute.

Sources indicate that in the 82nd minute, Sávio cut in from the flank and scored with a shot past Charlton goalkeeper Tiernan Brooks. He and the Spurs crowd thought he had a second a few minutes later, but his shot hit Ben Davies on its way into the net and the defender was credited with the goal.

Having sung for Moore earlier in the game, the Spurs fans wasted no time in trying out their new song for Sávio, inspired by the Spandau Ballet hit Gold.

Moore has been expected to move to Cologne on loan, but provided a reminder of his talent by opening the scoring in the first half with only his second goal for the club.

According to recent reports, what a hit from Mikey Moore! ⚪ pic.twitter.com/OgSM4qhiqs.

“We have to understand the best solution,” De Zerbi mentioned. “I would like to keep him. He’s young but a good player, but we can’t make the wrong decision. He needs to play, he needs to get games inside him.”.

Cutting in from the right, where Sávio is primed to play, Moore surged past his marker and shot from just inside the box. Brooks should have stopped it, but the ball flew past him and into the net.

Three minutes after Moore’s opener, Dominic Solanke scored his first goal since March to offer a reminder of what he can still give De Zerbi, who is poised to welcome Omar Marmoush to Tottenham.

Buoyed by his first-half goal, Moore skipped his way around a couple of tackles at the start of the second period but his low cross was cut out. The Spurs fans responded by singing “he’s one of our own.”.

Substitute Kevin Danso netted with his first touch from a header, before Sávio was introduced to steal the show, despite a late consolation goal from Charlton’s Lloyd Jones.

The victory set up a tough third-round trip to Anfield to face Liverpool for Tottenham, but De Zerbi noted: “It’s a great game. If we want to win the competition we have to win the games.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes in this competition, it can happen that you play against big teams. It’s a great challenge for the players, for me, for our clubs. We have to arrive ready to play in our style, with personality, ready to play a game following the work we are doing on the training ground.”.

“I do not know if I am the right man [to get the most out of Savio], but for sure he has to achieve. I think a player who is so good in one-on-one, so good at creating chances to score, to be complete, he has to score. If you analyse the other best wingers in the world, many of them, they score 10 to 15 goals per season. He has the qualities. Maybe his habits, he has to change habits, because he has to be focused on the assists, the one-on-one dribbling and also to score.”.

Omar Marmoush is closing in on an initial loan deal from Manchester City but that move is not complete and thus he is not available for Tottenham tonight. Micky van der Ven and Pedro Porro are both available having missed Tottenham’s loss at Brentford but the hosts are still without Xavi Simons, Pape Sarr, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert.

In a recent development, charlton have made the perfect start to their Championship campaign; a 2-1 home win over Derby was followed up by a 2-1 victory at recently-relegated West Ham. Nathan Jones’ side earned their place in the League Cup second round with a 3-1 win at Cheltenham in the first round.

“We have to be very organised and very professional, they [Tottenham] are a top team,” Jones said. “They have a great manager and a brilliant group of players. They already had a Premier League squad and they have spent, what is reaching about, I do not know, £300 million or something like that. It is a wonderful test, we have to be right near our best and do both sides of the game very well. Of course, you want to test yourself against the best managers and you want to test yourself against the best teams. For us, this is not our priority, the Championship is our priority, but this is the next game and therefore it is the most important.”.

Access, Not Chances: How Como Took Manchester United Apart – LC

📅 24 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game.
  • In a recent development, cesc Fàbregas’s side highlighted two things that rarely go together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 24.10.2026 in den Kategorien Champions League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

Como beat Manchester United 4-1 — and in this case the scoreline really is a fair expression of the game. For long stretches the match was one-sided, not in terms of chance volume but in terms of access: Como dictated in every phase where the ball went, who received it, and under what conditions it had to be played on. United never got on terms in any of those phases.

In a recent development, cesc Fàbregas’s side highlighted two things that rarely go together. Out of possession, a pressing structure with clear direction, isolation of one side, and man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress while everything around it was already speculating on the second ball. And in possession, a positional game of remarkable technical maturity that ties opponents in, switches play, and works systematically into the space behind them. The 4-1 is therefore less an outlier than evidence of work that has been built up over recent seasons.

This analysis goes through the phases one by one: first Como in possession and United’s response, then the work against the ball from the high press to defending the box, and finally the goals.

It has been revealed that in build-up, Como moved away from their nominal 4-2-3-1 and sat closer to a 4-3-3, with the eights as the real variable: very free in their movement and above all active in the half-spaces. The base structure stayed stable — a flat four plus a six in front of them, sometimes ahead of the line, sometimes slightly behind the forward line.

Close to their own goal, Como consistently involved goalkeeper Butez as an additional central player in the build-up. That created a five-against-four against United’s front line — awkward on paper, more awkward still in execution, because Como didn’t use the overload to play through but to tie opponents in. From there, the same shape kept appearing on both the right and the left: centre-back, full-back, a player from the half-position in the eight space, and a six alongside. A diamond that wasn’t an end in itself but had a purpose: the diagonal route out.

It has been revealed that como’s build-up structure. From a 4-1 (flat four), the half-positions with Paz and Perrone are added. Small triangles and diamonds emerge. The three attackers ahead of them create additional options in behind.

One detail deserves particular attention. At times the full-backs stood not wide but flat, in a half-position. That sounds like a nuance, but it had a clear function: it vacated the wing and created the space the eights could drop into — Paz and Perrone did so regularly. If you don’t occupy the wing yourself, you force the opponent to guard it anyway.

ManU got no access near the ball and left large diagonal spaces open on the far side.

Recent findings suggest that for United’s midfielders this was close to unsolvable. Tielemans, Mount and Andrey Santos spent the whole game struggling to establish any responsibility at all, let alone get into duels. When an eight dropped out, they couldn’t follow, and if one of them was tied in by it, a two-against-one opened up on the far wing. Como didn’t create that situation once; they created it serially.

The decisive mechanism lay in receiving and relaying the ball. The player in the deeper position usually worked with two touches: the first took the ball backwards, the second relayed it to the free teammate. At the end of every one of those actions stood a player with the game in front of him — and from that open position he could switch play.

It has been revealed that what made it possible were the preparatory movements. Paz and captain Da Cunha first lured their markers in the wrong direction and then worked with the head start they’d bought. That head start isn’t only space, it’s above all time: time to control the ball first and relay it second, rather than having to do both in one touch.

According to recent reports, A scene in the 17th minute is typical. Mason Mount steps out, Mazraoui goes into the duel at the same time — nominally United are in an overload here. Only neither of them really gets to the opponent, because both are too late. Paz can therefore calmly take his touch backwards and switch play directly with the second, dissolving the pressure before it had even formed.

When the build-up ran down the right, it highlighted in a recurring pattern: Paz and Da Cunha took the first touch backwards or inside and then switched with the left foot out of a closed body position. The players they found were systematically in open positions — Milla, the far-side six, or the wing-to-wing connection directly.

In the second half, Como adjusted the shape and more often played with two sixes, to form the diamonds faster and switch to the far-side six faster. Couto stood out in this: the right-back repeatedly played the chip into the six or ten space — six or seven times in a row during one spell. It was mainly Paz who received the ball there and could launch the attack.

In the second half Como focus on those diagonal spaces and look for them mainly with chipped balls.

It has been revealed that especially striking inside the diamond are the rotations between the players. Because of the connections between them, they moved in rotation depending on running path, space and ball movement. The same recurring spaces were re-occupied. Under pressure on the ball carrier, the outer players pushed flat or ran in behind the opponents; the highest player in the diamond burst out of the cover shadow and became the reference point in depth. On a deep pass, the two wide players released and joined the depth, able to offer themselves again immediately in an open body position. If the pass went via the flat wide players, the spaces in front of the upcoming ball carrier could be run into. Every rotation, every positional adjustment was coordinated with the others and, in the end, produced a stream of pressure-resolving passes while Manchester United chased the press in vain.

Recent findings suggest that como bridged the middle third exceptionally rapidly, via dribbles at speed and diagonal passes. Behind it stood a recognisable principle: first tie the opponent to one wing, then get behind them via the diagonal, and in the final third do the same thing again. In sum, that produced the shape of a Z — build-up on the right, transition on the left, finish from the right again.

Industry observers note that in this example Como pin ManU in the press with their short passing. Thanks to the extra attacker on the ball-near side they can play through the pressure and switch.

According to recent reports, the connections between wingers and striker carried these attacks and were deliberately kept flexible. The wide players sometimes stayed wide, sometimes came short, sometimes tucked inside. Douvikas accordingly either waited deep in front of the line for the chipped ball or, when space opened up on the wing, received the deeper pass and then ran in behind along the wing as soon as the ball sat on the full-back’s open foot. That flexibility produced the overloads on one side, and the overloads produced the central overload.

Recent findings suggest that in the final third one element was added that is rare in fast transition teams: patience. Como drew opponents towards them with dribbles and short passes, used back-passes when needed, and then switched in front of the block. Da Cunha, Baturina and Paz were the three who could tie opponents in and then find the diagonal. They created the positions on the diagonal, were available to receive, and used their space to apply pressure. The block was usually tied in with short touches, the switch and the position behind the opponent prepared, and quick finishes sought.

Sources indicate that the intensity in possession shouldn’t be underestimated. Practically every attack involved at least three or four players, the width was occupied, the centre likewise, and there were multiple options throughout. What they looked for almost every time was the space behind the opponent on the far side — exactly the zone that is closed last when a block shifts across.

Paz brought the right profile for this pattern. A strong left foot cutting inside from the right, he repeatedly dropped into the right-hand blind side of his opponents, got shots away there with few touches, and racked up the most shots of the match. That the finishes generally came off few touches isn’t a detail but the consequence of the time won further back.

As the move continues, Como again look for the blind side of the defenders. Here Douvikas and Paz are positioned in behind, with Da Cunha joining in front of the back line. After briefly pinning the opponents, the switch reaches Da Cunha, who misses the target from distance.

What carries all of this is the technical execution. Soft passes, sharp ones when the moment called for it, consistently well timed and played into the right foot — for ninety minutes. Passing that secure at that tempo is what makes a variable concept actually retrievable.

United’s basic problem out of possession was the hybrid. They pressed half man-oriented, but with a plus-one in the last line — a construction that forces compromises in both directions. It demands access up front that it doesn’t fund at the back.

There were certainly moments when it worked. When Dalot pushed through into the press on the right and passed his man backwards, a clean man-orientation emerged all the way up to the front — and with it a clear assignment for Mount, out of which the ball could be won. But that stayed the exception. Most of the time Dalot sat too flat out of possession, so United couldn’t trigger the duels up front and went into the press a man short.

Mount was the most conspicuous case in this respect. He barely got into a duel across the whole match because the decision to step out always came too late. Against a team that works with preparatory movements, a late decision is practically the same as none: the opponent already has the head start before the journey even begins.

Industry observers note that on top of that came a problem on the far side. There, United’s winger frequently failed to protect the depth — usually Mbeumo, who jogged back rather than closing the space. But that was precisely the target zone of Como’s diagonal switches. It allowed them to change sides almost at will and regularly find an open structure on the other side.

Recent findings suggest that the second half brought no improvement. The distances to opponents stayed large, and centrally what was actually intended still didn’t materialise. Michael Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring more physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it didn’t solve the problem — the assignments still didn’t work, the duels in the centre still didn’t happen, and the wide positions dragged the eights out further, which opened new spaces.

Sources indicate that in the end the energy simply wasn’t there to press with the necessary intensity. United’s press became increasingly static, and a static press against an opponent with this passing quality yields not a single ball win — it only hands them the starting positions they’re looking for anyway.

Como started the game in a high press and sustained it above all in the first half, with isolated spells after the break too. It was triggered on back-passes and goal kicks — and, remarkably, by their own goals: after every strike the team immediately pushed high again instead of managing the lead in a deeper block.

It has been revealed that the steering ran consistently towards United’s left build-up side. The reason is personnel: Harry Maguire played there with his weaker left foot as the outside foot, and next to him stood another right-footer in Noussair Mazraoui on the left. Two right-footers on one build-up side means the ball always has to be taken back inside to play on — exactly where Como were closing the door. The press was usually triggered by the left-sided forward, with the ball ending up at either Maguire or Mazraoui.

Pressing structure after the change in the second half.

Industry observers note that in the centre Como defended man-oriented, with both sixes pushing very high and taking flat passes into United’s midfielders out of the game. That removed the short route through the middle as an option and left the long ball. But the long ball triggered nothing for United: the second balls went to Como practically every time.

That isn’t chance, it’s running work. The sixes consistently tracked the negative pressing paths back, anticipated the long ball early, and were in front of the line before it arrived. Luis Milla covered the most ground of any player on the pitch in this pattern — recovery runs after being played past, doubling up on the ball, attacking the second ball. When the long ball came from Maguire or one of the full-backs, a six was regularly in front of the line with an intense sprint, sealing the centre, taking away the diagonal follow-up passes and attacking the loose balls.

Defending the long ball and extra support on the second ball.

Recent findings suggest that once the ball was on one side, that side was isolated. The near-side forward had access to the centre-back and dropped back a touch when the pass went to the full-back, so that he covered centre-back and six simultaneously and closed the square pass. The far-side forward marked the goalkeeper. That served two functions at once: it took away United’s escape route via the keeper along with the switch, and it kept a player in position for the moment of the turnover.

The double pivot worked in a deliberate half-position. The near-side six stayed tight to his man, the far-side one dropped slightly behind him — securing the space and at the same time establishing access to the far-side centre-back in United’s back three.

Recent findings suggest that the last line defended largely man-for-man in the high press, and very tightly. But the decisive detail is the one that carries the whole concept: the man-marking near the ball applied only to the action in progress. Around it, players were already releasing from their assignments and orienting towards the second ball. That is only retrievable at very high intensity — and it’s the reason United’s forced long balls produced not a single usable moment.

When Como dropped a line, the man-orientation at the second height stayed exceptionally high. Here too the back-pass served as the trigger to push up as a unit and tip back into man-marking. If United were in a closed body position, the Comaschi had already pushed up far enough to attack the back-pass at the moment it was played — a pattern that led directly to the 3-0. The half-position was at work there again: closing down level with the centre-back while simultaneously prepared to push through onto the next player deeper.

Industry observers note that in the first half Como still had problems assigning the half-positions against ManU’s 3-2-5. In this example Fernandes moves to the wing, Como fail to establish responsibility and access and are played through at mid-height.

Up to half-time, though, Como had a structural problem with this. The pure man-marking didn’t come off cleanly, because of the two sixes in front of the line, one should really have tucked in and taken over the half-position for the centre-backs. That didn’t happen consistently. The consequence: a centre-back stepped out, the space behind him stayed unoccupied, and that was exactly what United kept attacking.

It has been revealed that the pattern of pressing onto Manchester United’s left side continued in the second half, now with Dalot at full-back. The press was still triggered by Douvikas, with the ball-near winger pushing up as a second striker to press the centre-back. Paz focused on the visitors’ ball-near six and Couto pushed through onto Dalot. Through the central connections the game was isolated on one side.

Sources indicate that at half-time Como adjusted. One six moved directly into the line, with the far-side winger pushing in onto the six — they now pressed out of a 5-2-1-2. Lucas Da Cunha pressed through from the right onto Maguire, while Nico Paz picked up United’s six. The central forward pressed the central centre-back and from there carried on to the goalkeeper. The far-side wide midfielder and the remaining six were poised — one onto United’s free six, one onto the far-side centre-back — again in that half-position between opponent and the space to be protected.

ManU building up high against the man-oriented Italians.

The effect was immediately visible. Como controlled the half-positions, got access right into the last line throughout, and set the rhythm of the match from then on. The adjustment solved exactly the problem the first half had left open, without changing the underlying principle.

Recent findings suggest that in the final phase Como defended from a very deep line inside the box. That left barely any space behind the line to play into — which United hardly looked for anyway. The visitors attacked little depth and rarely occupied the width in the final third, so Como could stay compact without being punished for it.

Sources indicate that accordingly, a lot of players stood very centrally in and in front of the box. That produced numerous cover shadows and a numerical superiority around the ball, which allowed them to steer actively within the block rather than merely react. At times they deliberately steered inside, to guide the opponent into the prepared congestion and cover from a deeper position.

Deep back line in the box, centre closed and play steered inside. The box defending allowed the English side shots from distance.

Recent findings suggest that the crucial point is that Como left the gaps open not despite this set-up but because of it. If you pack the box and secure the depth, you give up the space in front of the line — and that is exactly where United were supposed to shoot from.

The numbers vindicate the decision. Taking the conceded goal out of the box, Como allowed nine shots from outside the penalty area across ninety minutes, worth roughly 0.24 xG combined; only three of them were even on target. On top of that, of the four shots inside the box, two came from at least 14 to 15 metres and effectively belong in the long-range category as well. United accepted the invitation, and the shooting quality was perfectly decent — it’s just that with that scoring probability over a whole match, the most likely outcome is precisely what happened.

Tracking the ball for the first goal.

1-0, Nico Paz (2′) — The goal comes before United are even set. Como take the goal kick rapidly and play straight to the full-back, luring the visitors into the press — only not cleanly. Mason Mount triggers the pressure and is played past, and on the second ball he goes into the duel as well instead of holding the middle and looking for the space where he could pick the ball up. That is exactly what opens the centre, the space for the second ball is there, and Paz can play it through.

Recent findings suggest that what follows is the transition principle in its purest form: a quick switch to the diagonal side, then short passes against a very deep line. Matheus Cunha doesn’t pick up the player behind him and leaves the ten space open, where Paz is standing. He needs two touches because neither Cunha from above nor Maguire from his distance gets into the duel. Lammens, for his part, doesn’t defend the goal with his cover shadow but takes the near post — which leaves the far corner to a strong left foot. The curled finish into it is quality, though.

Industry observers note that 2-0, Anastasios Douvikas (49′, assist Paz) — Same zone, same cause. Bryan Mbeumo doesn’t choose to shut the centre but closes the centre-back, which creates the space for Da Cunha, who drives forward and plays Martin Baturina in. Centrally, Mount again fails to pick up his man. Out wide, Amad Diallo, introduced at half-time, generates no pressure centrally, so Mazraoui can’t take over the deep wide player in the first place.

The result is Paz behind the opponent, in the ten space, dribbling unopposed at goal. Matthijs de Ligt establishes no reference to Douvikas’s run in behind and slips as well — a one-against-one with the goalkeeper that Douvikas finishes coolly.

3-0, Nico Paz (57′) — The only goal that comes directly out of the work against the ball. Como are in the midfield press in a closed position with access to the inside lane, win the ball there and punish a lapse of concentration in the visitors’ build-up. At the end, Paz is alone in front of Lammens again.

4-0, Jacobo Ramón (76′, assist Kaiki) — This goal comes from a longer possession spell and shows the assignment problem in its clearest form. Mazraoui is too narrow and has no access to the wide player. Diallo stands in the space with access to neither the central player nor the full-back nor the winger — an orientation that doesn’t work in any direction.

According to recent reports, como switch to Máximo Perrone, who can slide the ball out wide because the space is simply free. From there comes the cross from an open body position, and in the centre Como run a two-against-one at the end of which Ramón scores.

4-1, Joshua Zirkzee (90′) — Como’s only lapse, and one in a phase in which the team had already dropped very deep. United get the ball to the wing, it’s two against two in the box, and the cross is initially only feinted. Zirkzee orients himself well forwards at that moment, while Como’s defenders are already stepping out after the feinted cross. Diallo’s ball in behind the line is strong, the offside call is razor-thin in his favour, and Zirkzee takes two touches before finishing one-against-one with the goalkeeper. A blemish, not a structural problem.

According to recent reports, the common denominator — Three of Como’s four goals come in the same zone: the space in front of and behind United’s line that nobody takes responsibility for. Mount is involved in two of those scenes through an assignment he never establishes, Diallo in two more after coming on. Nico Paz is at the heart of three of the four goals, twice as scorer, once as the provider — always out of the opponent’s blind side.

Sources indicate that como’s 4-1 has one common cause across every phase, and it lies less in any single idea than in its execution under continuous load. Out of possession they steered, isolated and speculated on the second ball — with man-marking that applied near the ball only for the action in progress and was already dissolved around it. In possession they tied opponents in, switched play and worked systematically into the space behind. Both require eleven players to anticipate a teammate’s decision, and both functioned over the full distance.

According to recent reports, the connecting detail is the half-position. In the press, the far-side six stood between opponent and the space to be protected; in possession, the eights worked out of the same zone, and the full-backs occupied it flat in order to vacate the wing for exactly those players. Como, in other words, occupied the position in both directions from which two jobs can be done at once — which is why the side could neither be played past in the press nor be pinned in the build-up.

Recent findings suggest that for United the diagnosis is more uncomfortable than the result. The problem wasn’t individual errors but that the team never, in any phase, got into the duels it needed. The mixture of half man-orientation and a plus-one in the last line funded no access up front, and without access every decision is made too late — from Mount in the centre to Mbeumo failing to secure the far-side depth. Carrick’s double change at half-time was meant to bring physicality to the six with Carlos Baleba, but it changed nothing about the assignments, and in Diallo a player came on wide who reached neither one opponent nor the other in his space. That the energy ran out in the end was a consequence rather than a cause.

In a recent development, that leaves the context. A 4-1 against Manchester United is no proof in itself, and Como’s finishing was exceptionally efficient on the night. What showed regardless of the result, though, is a team with a recognisable, rehearsed answer in all four phases of the game — and one that put a technical maturity on the pitch in possession that you wouldn’t readily credit to a side promoted two years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Après avoir affronté et péniblement éliminé la meilleure attaque de National 1, Sainté va défier samedi (19h) dans le Chaudron la pire défense de Ligue 3.

En effet, si l’ASSE a sur le papier le tirage le moins favorable des clubs de Ligue 2 (les 11 autres rescapés affrontent des clubs de N1, N2 ou Regionale), on notera que Villefranche est bien mal en point dans sa division. Au point que le club situé 30km au nord de Lyon a changé de coach début octobre, en enrôlant Hakim Malek (ex-coach de Martigues alors en L2).

Actuellement 17e sur 18 avec 2 victoires, 2 nuls et déjà 9 défaites, Villefranche s’est incliné (2-4) ce week-end à Bastia, alors que le club semblait aller un peu mieux depuis l’arrivée de Malek qui, avant cette défaite avait pris 4pts en 3 matchs de championnat et battu aisément Paray le monial (formation de R2) en Coupe (3-0).

It has been revealed that néanmoins, avec 30 buts encaissés en 13 matchs (soit 8 de plus que la 2e pire défense de la L3 !), Villefranche bat des records, bien au-delà de la pire défense de L2 (Rodez, 24 buts encaissés) et de L1 (Auxerre et Le Havre, 25 buts encaissés), mais également plus que toute autre équipe de N1 ou N2 (qui ont certes disputé moins de journées). Outre la défaite à Bastia, deux autres fessées subies à l’extérieur en septembre à Fleury (1-6) et au Puy (1-4) confirment en particulier la fragilité des Caladois loin de chez eux.

Cette très poreuse défense ne nous est pas totalement inconnue puisqu’y évoluent deux anciens verts (Marvin Tshibuabua très récemment rejoint par Maedine Makhloufi prêté par Dunkerque) qu'on imagine très motivés à l'idée de faire mentir ces chiffres.

#166107. The madness of Liverpool’s first foray into European competition
